utterances.text: Moving to a second map - and I'll do this as quickly as I can - you also made some markings on a -- a map of the Gjakove area during the course of the interview. Do you recall doing that? The second map.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this is an A4 size piece of paper, Your Honours. It looks like that, and it should be attached to the 92 bis package. Now, it's this map in particular that's extremely hard to read, and I have discussed with the amici the fact that the Court may well be assisted by a computer-generated map, and I will ask some questions about that. And you don't have that yet, but I propose to make some sense of this by using a computer-generated improvement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, sir, this map that you now have with -- bearing ERN number K0223471, you see that map?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that a map of?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: This is a map of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you, during the course of the interview, make some markings, some handwritten markings, on this map; draw some circles, draw some dates, draw some arrows?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And have you, during the course of the interview yesterday been shown some computer-generated documents and compared them to the markings you made on this map? Were you shown some documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps we could distribute those. I'm going to be asking that the Court accept them, but -- with my friend's permission. But the accused, although it's been disclosed to them in the past, they haven't been marked as an exhibit, but they would certainly assist the Court in understanding his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like a copy of each of these maps, please, placed on the ELMO. The first one is the one with the red sort of orangey circle, which is a photocopy of the map that was attached to the 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir. This is a copy of the same map upon which you made markings earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the area circled in red on this map, is that the area of Decani that you were trying to describe in the course of your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, entirely. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might the witness now be shown a second map with some markings on it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now asking you to now look at the map now placed on the ELMO. This is again an enlarged portion of the map that you drew your personal markings on. Have you, yesterday, had an opportunity to compare the notations you made with the computer-generated markings on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell the Court about whether or not this map accurately depicts what you were trying to draw on the map produced into evidence earlier? How does it compare?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Entirely the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With reference to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These should have separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that now. First of all, I take it you want to deal with the photocopy of the whole municipality with the various figures on it which is illegible but no doubt you would like it exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would have the next exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that map is actually included in the 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no, but give it a separate number now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 143.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And next, the map with the red on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 143.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And finally, the one with the various markings on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honour, Prosecutor's Exhibit 143.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in the course of your statement, you made some markings on Exhibit 143.4, the one that is before you on the ELMO. Can you describe for us, if you would, please, very briefly, what the red arrows signify.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The red arrows mark the displacement of the population and their movements in the direction of Gjakove from the valley of Carragojs and from the village of Korenica towards Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And maybe you could use your pointer because there are two red arrows, tell us which red arrow refers to which. You are now talking about the one starting near the stop and working down towards the bottom. Yes. Diagonal line.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The longest red arrow shows the movement of the population from the Carragojs Valley, as it's called, towards the village of Meja and to Gjakove. And on the left, the curved red arrow shows the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: -- displacement of the population towards Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The blue arrow, which seems to be parallel to the first of the two red arrows, which -- what does that signify?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The blue arrow shows the direction of the attack of the special forces of the MUP, and alongside it, there's another arrow in green which shows the direction of the attack of the military forces belonging to the 63rd Parachute Brigade from Nis. And on the right and on the left, these green lines, thick green lines, show the blockade of the entire territory by military forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've described that in your statement, have you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. And these circles --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. First of all --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: -- in green --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the green circle where there is a black box indicating an arrow to it, what does that circle mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The command of the operation consisting of officers of the army, which commanded operations in the field, was sited here in the place called Qafa e Osekut. That's the name of the hill. And from here, you can see the entire territory in which this operation was conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there for a minute and ask you this question: Where were you on the 27th of April, 1999, when you indicated in your statement that you saw these things happening? Where were you located, physically located in order to be able to draw these arrows?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: On the 27th, in the morning, I arrived from Nis. And when I heard from my brother what was happening there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me focus the question. Where physically were you, standing or sitting or whatever you were doing, when you were able to observe? Where were you physically?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Physically, when I saw these things, I was in Meja and in Korenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This place called Osek, were you ever there on the 27th of April? Or the 28th?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No. On the 27th, I was not at the Qafa e Osekut. I was there on the 28th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: And also in the village of Duzhnje and Nec, on same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. When you were in Osek on the 28th, could you see the things that you have described for us, this vantage point?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I was at this vantage point myself, and I taught there for some time with Colonel Kotur and with Colonel Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Colonel Kotur belongs to the command of the Pristina Corps, and Colonel Stankovic was the chief of the brigade, the army brigade, of course, in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Which led the operations in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand who you were with, I understand who they are, that's in your statement. What I want to -- what I'm trying to direct your mind to is when you were physically at that location with those people, what could you see happening down in the valley? First of all, could you see the valley?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see the movement of these people that you've described?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: On the 28th, there was no movement at all because the people were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already entirely displaced on the 27th in the morning. You could only see smoke and flames coming from almost all the houses in the valley of Carragojs and beyond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And on the 28th, did you see the movement of the forces you've described, the military and MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, the second day of the operation, because the operation covered about half of the territory, and it continued on a second day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have only two more questions, sir, about the map, because the rest of the evidence is contained in your statements. I know the temptation is to tell us more, but Their Honours have this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the map the witness is mentioning in his second statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I know you put the number, paragraph 59, or the third paragraph of page 12. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just check, because this statement, before it was bis'd was not paragraph numbered. We did that for ease of identification, as we indicated to the Court, that we would try to number the paragraphs. So I'm just going to have to double-check that. And there's two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Second one, 59 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 59 paragraph in the new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It is the one for 59. The annotated map of the operation in the Carragojs Valley and Meja area. This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Paragraph 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two more questions, if I may. The red circles. You haven't told us what these red circles on this exhibit, 143.4, I believe.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The red circle, the first one from the top is a checkpoint that was in the village of Meja. And the second one was at the crossroads of the road from Meja to Korenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for reference, what happened at those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: At these checkpoints, more than 500 people were stopped at Meja by police forces, regular police forces, local police, paramilitaries, and some other reservists who were also there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: And at -- may I go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on, because we have much to do today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, and could you also describe for us, please, on this map where Meja is. You've made reference in your statements to Meja and incidents in Meja. Is Meja actually depicted on this map, and if so, where? Could you point to it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Meja is on the left side of the red circle. I've covered that -- the name with the red circle a bit, but you can see clearly written "Meja."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There are two red circles. It is the top red circle with the bottom part of the red circle obliterating the word; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There's a line, and you can see, in brackets "Meja."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those are all the questions I have. With the Court's indulgence, I'll quickly, for the benefit, read in a very brief summary of what is contained in the two lengthy statements. My understanding, Your Honours, from the statements is that the witness describes that from December of 1998, he was an officer in the Air Defence and Rocket Artillery Brigade of the Pristina Corps. And then in 1999, General Pavkovic was appointed commander of the VJ 3rd Army, while General Lazarevic took over as commander of the Pristina Corps. In his statements, the witness describes in some detail an overview of the structure of the armed forces, including the VJ, the MUP, and a structure he termed Territorial Defence, the TO. He indicates that he is of the view that during times of war, the MUP and TO came under the control of the VJ. Paramilitary groups, including Arkan's Tigers, Seselj's White Eagles, and Franko Simatovic's unit, the Frenkis, operated under the TO. His statement indicates that the regular VJ in the Gjakove area was responsible for operations against the KLA, and that attacks against civilian targets were conducted by the MUP. His statement describes a huge influx of army and police between February and March of 1999. In addition to these units, the witness will describe the creation of local police operating in various villages where the regular MUP had difficulty patrolling. Now, it goes on to say that after NATO began bombing, groups of 5 to 10 people would arrive in Kosovo where they would join up with VJ units. He indicates that they appeared unkempt and many had criminal records. He then describes that VJ reservists wore the same green camouflage uniforms and insignia as the VJ but, of course, these reservists tended to be older. The MUP reservists were usually people with military police background and retired regular MUP. He says that there were about 50 to 70 in Djakovica, but many more came from Serbia. At first, the MUP were tasked to handle the KLA alone. They wore blue camouflage uniforms and had a patch that included the colours of the Serbian flag and the word "Milicija." The TO included people ranging in age from 15 to 65 years. They were not VJ or MUP, but included Civil Defence people. And their role, apparently, was to defend the civilian population. He indicates that partial mobilisation of the TO began in October and November of 1998 and was complete by January or February of 1999. He indicates there were paramilitaries in the area, most of whom were Arkan's and Seselj's groups, with about 30 from Frenki's group. And he goes on to say that, in theory, all armed groups were subordinate to the VJ. The VJ and the MUP met every day but they had separate headquarters. Now, operations maps showing deployments were prepared by the VJ and then given to the MUP, and the MUP relied on the VJ support for large operations. He goes on to say that at the start of March 1999, an operation was planned against Albanians in the area, and describes in the statement being present at a meeting where an order was given that at least 100 heads had to be eliminated and all houses burnt in retribution for the killing of a MUP officer in a KLA ambush. On the 27th of April, a massacre at Meja and Korenica took place. On the 28th of April, 1999, the day after the massacre at Meja, the witness was in brigade headquarters where he saw a report on which -- in which the VJ stated that 74 terrorists had been killed in Korenica and 68 in Meja. On the day of the massacre, the witness helped ten families to escape. He helped them pass through a checkpoint manned by the MUP. After the massacre, he saw about 20 bodies that had been shot from close range. He notes that he saw the powder burns on the heads. The following day, the witness assisted a further two families to escape by assuring the MUP that they were not KLA members. The witness recognised members of paramilitaries groups in Meja at the time of the massacre and describes that the factions that took part in this massacre included the VJ, MUP, local police, and paramilitaries. Now, the witness also produced the annotated maps as an attachment to his statements. We've gone into that information in some detail, both with the Carragojs Valley, and Meja. And the VJ was in the west in order to defend against the KLA coming from Albania and was also deployed along the Djakovice-Decani road. The military moved down the valley, burning property and pushing civilians towards paramilitary groups around Meja. These paramilitary groups acted as a blocking force. This operation was coordinated from the headquarters in Djakovica. On the 27th of April, the push reached a place where the local MUP and paramilitaries took over. The massacre occurred on the same day, and on the 28th of April, the push continued in a south-easterly direction. And that is clearly visible from these maps that we discussed. In the days after the massacre, the VJ and MUP were looking for bulldozers ostensibly for road clearance, but the witness opines that it was for the disposal of bodies. And the reason he says that, apparently, is that on the 29th of April, he saw two trucks going toward Djakovica from Meja, covered with tarpaulins. When the tarpaulins lifted in the wind, the witness saw parts of bodies. The KLA, according to him, had left Djakovica area by the time NATO commenced their bombing. And from the beginning of 1999, there was no real resistance from the KLA in the area. In these various statements, the witness also names key individuals in the VJ, the MUP, the TO, and the municipality, and he outlines their roles during the period of the NATO bombing. Clearly, this is only the briefest of outlines of fairly detailed evidence, but Your Honours have that for your consideration. Those are my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military court in Nis convicted you to a prison sentence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were sentenced to a prison term of 15 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: This is what I heard. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of that, were you not able to move around, to move outside the region you're in?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No. I could move about. Wherever I wanted to go, I went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could move around freely outside Kosovo and Metohija, all through the territory of Yugoslavia; is that it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I can go even to the territory of Serbia, but I will return without my head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But then that means, in view of the sentence, that in fact you are not permitted and cannot move outside Kosovo in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Only me, but no one wished to go there and end up in prison or end up with his head -- beheaded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, this circumstance, what you've just been explaining to us, and the fact that you were sentenced to a serious term of imprisonment, that you were in detention and a warrant was published, issued for your arrest, now, all these facts, do they motivate you to testify here in the capacity of a witness, a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I am not at all sad about that. The court there can do what they deem appropriate. I don't feel ill at ease, because I have done nobody any harm. I have only performed my duties in the exercise of my duties in the Yugoslav army under the constitution, to defend the people and the state and not to engage in other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Does this fact and these circumstances that you explained to us, that is to say, that you would end up without a head or in prison if you went there, and the fact that you were sentenced to a maximum prison sentence according to the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, that you got 15 years, in fact, was that a motive for you to come and be a Prosecution witness at this trial?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that you went about your constitutional business and duties and that you defended the country as an officer of Yugoslavia. Who did you defend the country from, in fact?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: We didn't need to defend the country, because under the constitution, the army was supposed to protect the country from any external attacks, but not to become active and fight against its own people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the country attacked from outside by the NATO aggressors or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: We tried to defend ourselves, but it was of no avail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who were you defending the country from?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In fact, we engaged in a meaningless defence, I would say, because it was quite meaningless to defend ourselves against the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who attacked Yugoslavia; NATO or the international community?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: NATO attacked, but it was under the supervision of international community. Everything that went on in Kosova and the former Yugoslavia was open for the entire world to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that mean that you claim that NATO attacked Yugoslavia upon permission by the Security Council of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a matter for this witness. No doubt if it's relevant, we can hear other evidence about it. You should restrict your examination to the matters which he can deal with, particularly his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that it is not the duty of the army to react against terrorism because that is an internal enemy. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: If there is terrorism, then there are forces that fight terrorism, and they are called anti-terrorist forces. But this is not done by the regular army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what I'm asking you. You consider that it is not the duty of the army to fight terrorism?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: We didn't have to do with any large-scale terrorism as to require the engagement of large units of the army. Then in that case, the police and other forces shouldn't have done anything when in fact they are paid precisely to fight such phenomena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, then, that when a terrorist group, for example, as you were an officer of the Yugoslav army, when a terrorist group attacks a unit of the Yugoslav army, then it is the army's duty to telephone the police to come and protect them from the terrorists? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No. But you cannot call an entire people terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who called an entire people terrorists? Did I say that, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: You can understand that, because the war was declared on the entire Albanian people of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who declared war on the Albanian people?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It was not openly declared, but in fact going by the way things occurred, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean the Albanians as part of the people of Yugoslavia against which NATO waged a war?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I'm not sure I got the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's have the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were an officer of the Yugoslav army, I assume that you are well acquainted with the rules and regulations governing the functioning of the Yugoslav army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I'm well acquainted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that, according to the rules, the army can be used in peacetime to combat terrorism?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. An army unit, yes, but not the whole army. In Kosova, all the army units that exist in Yugoslavia were used. Only the navy was not used, and the ships. Otherwise, all the arm -- all the units, the physical -- the troops and the military equipment were used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you claim, therefore, that the whole army, the entire Yugoslav army, was used in Kosovo in the struggle against terrorism. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I know very well like the cases in Nis, Vranje, Kraljevo, Cacak, in the barracks there were only some guards and a very small number of soldiers. All the others were deployed in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact and from what you said in your statement, there are three armies of the ground forces in Yugoslavia, that is, the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The 3rd Army was -- was -- included also the Pristina Corps, but I'm talking about that because from Vojvodina, including the whole of Serbia, with a minimal -- with the exception of the minimal forces were there, the others were sent to Kosova to fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware, as an officer, although a deserter, albeit, from the Yugoslav army, that Yugoslavia was threatened by a ground invasion?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you claim that the 1st Army and the 2nd Army, that all of them went to Kosovo, and the whole of the 3rd Army as well.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I answered earlier. If I can add up to it: In Kosova there were also army units from the Republika Srpska. They were stationed west of Gjakove, in the place called Rezina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we've cleared that up. You say that the entire Yugoslav army was sent to Kosovo. Let's move on to my next questions. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Over 150.000 forces were there, according to some figures I've heard also my former colleagues, officers who were in high positions. And you know very well that the army was cut down, downsized, according to an agreement that you had yourself signed. After what happened in Kosova, everybody was sent to Kosova, leaving behind only the most indispensable number to carry out the usual duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not aware, therefore, of the fact that the army is increased in times of war. More soldiers are sent. You know nothing about that, as an officer?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. There was also a mobilisation, a mass mobilisation in Serbia. And people who didn't want to come and fight were put in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as an officer, is that something that seems strange to you, that when a country is exposed to aggression, that one mobilises the army?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's not strange. However, it's strange and quite -- it's quite understandable that people should refuse to come and fight in Kosova in a war that is entirely meaningless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know that. That's just what you're claiming. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's true that people were imprisoned because they didn't agree to go to war in Kosova. Another truth is that soldiers deserted from the ranks of the army and even fled abroad in order to -- not to be involved in a war that was quite senseless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As you're a military deserter and were condemned to a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prison term, do you consider that anywhere in the world there is an army which does not arrest deserters from the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's an irrelevant question. You've made the point about the prison sentence by the military court. There's no need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left the Yugoslav army only three days before the NATO forces entered Kosovo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I was with them until three days before the Yugoslav army withdrew. I stayed in Kosova, and I didn't have any need to go with them. I was on the brink of retirement, and the war was almost over. I had nothing to look for in Serbia or any other country. I only wanted to stay in my birthplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question aimed at pinpointing the time when you ceased to be an active officer in the army or, rather, the time you actually left the Yugoslav army. That was what I was getting at. So in terms of time, that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't flee anywhere. I stayed exactly where my unit was, where my birthplace was, and where my apartment was. I didn't leave my country at all. In fact, I didn't leave the place where I was born; Kosova. That's where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When did you leave the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three days -- until three days before the Yugoslav army left Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right after the end of the war, you had meetings with the KLA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And otherwise, up until then, you were on the KLA's list for liquidation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How don't you know when on page 14, paragraph 4 of your one but last statement of the 12th to the 15th of February, 2002, that's what it says? How come you knew then and you don't know now?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know that I was on any list. Maybe they wrote lists. They made various lists. I have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I told you the portion of your statement where you say that you do know you were on the list of the KLA for liquidation, but I don't want to argue with you. What I want to do is to ask you questions. You went for talks with the KLA on several occasions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't seek to go to talk to the KLA, but they came to me and asked to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not discussing the question of at whose request was the meeting held. I'm just noting that you did go to a meeting with the KLA on several occasions. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand the relevance of this to my statement, because we met after the war and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must be the judges of that. Did you have any meetings with the KLA before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the war, I never had contact with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nor during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said yourself, but we're going to get to that later, you warned the KLA to move away so that they would not be destroyed in one particular action. That is what you mentioned yourself in your statement. I'm also referring to several meetings you had with the KLA after you deserted. You attended such talks several times; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: After the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among others, you talked with the chief of the KLA police in the region or, rather, in the area of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you say in your statement, you talked to Ramush Haradinaj, as well. Tell me, how many times did the KLA talk to you, including that meeting when you saw Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I know Ramush Haradinaj as a person, but I have never spoken to him in my life, nor has he spoken to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's on page 16, the last paragraph of the statement given between the 12th and 15th of February, 2001. But let's leave that aside. How many times did you have these talks with the KLA? How many times altogether?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I met the KLA in their own offices after the war on three occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met with the KLA on three occasions after the war? Not to mention the contact during the war. So now let us put this all together through the following question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't go too fast. He denies any contact with the KLA during the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, I'm not going to put a question in relation to that. Its turn will come. I'm only go to ask about what the witness confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have this conviction to the highest prison sentence possible. That was a ruling by the military court in Nis. That is one fact. Secondly, you were on the list for liquidations by the KLA. And thirdly, you said that you had three rounds of talks with the KLA. Do you think that all of this makes it clear that you came here to testify at somebody's request, like the KLA? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: This is not true at all. I have come here because of the lamenting and the tears of the families, brothers and sisters, mothers who have been left without their loved ones, who have come to me and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. Let him finish. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who have come to me, many of them, and have asked me don't I know something about the fate of their loved ones, because I was in the army. So it was a moral duty for me to tell you something about these things. And I can meet with the KLA and talk with them. I can meet with whom I want and talk with them now, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you claim that this statement is not your life insurance policy for the rest of your life that is ahead of you? Under the circumstances that I've just mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I will never forget the crimes and terrible things that I have seen and which happened in the places I mentioned in my statement, committed by forces of the Yugoslav army, MUP, paramilitaries and others. Though less in the army and more by the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you. But is it, therefore, your claim that you came to testify here and that nobody threatened you, nobody blackmailed you, nobody brought any pressure to bear upon you? Is that what you claim?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I have not come to testify here under any kind of pressure from anybody. I have not come here to lie. And everything that I can say I say with a full sense of conscience and I am ready to face up to anybody -- anybody's questions, and I have simply come here to tell the truth and not to do anything else and merely to say the things that I have seen myself and heard with my own ears.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All these circumstances that we've referred to, the conviction, the liquidation list, and the meetings, that is not pressure upon you, according to what you've said. Now my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've already put this. And, Mr. Milosevic, one of the ways we waste time is by your repeating things. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't you worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When giving your statements, you were interviewed, among other people, by Philip Coo, a military analyst, that is, and he will be a witness during the trial. Number 74, I believe. Was this testimony or this statement given attended by somebody from the KLA as well?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember. And do you remember where this interview was held?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know about which interview you're talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your interview when you gave a statement to military analyst Philip Coo, who took your statement. Where was this?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know about giving any statement to a military analyst or nothing like that. If you're talking about my two statements given to the respected Court here, I can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The statement of the February 2001, where was that given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement, he was a representative of the Tribunal, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Where was the statement made? You made a statement, you were interviewed in February 2001. The question is whereabouts were you interviewed and where did you make your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the building of the driving school in Gjakove. About five minutes away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what is now in this building of the driving school in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's now the UNMIK police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that where the station of this so-called Kosovo Protection Corps is as well? Because they are together with UNMIK.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They're not in one place. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who attended that interview of yours?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember at least how many persons were present while you were speaking to Philip Coo?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know this name at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be of assistance if the name were properly pronounced. I'm not claiming any attempted deception but it may be fairer to the witness. The cover sheets of the statements indicate who were present, by name, and the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Philip Coo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Paulo Pastore Stocchi. And the interpreter, Iris Rutari-Coen. Those, and it says, "Names of all persons present during the interviews," again Paulo Pastore Stocchi, Philip Coo, and Iris Rutari-Coen. On the earlier statement, we have the same interviewer, Paulo Pastore Stocchi, and a different interpreter, and it says, "Names of all persons present during interviews," and this would be the -- sorry, the 200 statement. There are two other individuals named, one of whom -- sorry, one other individual named who is brother-in-law of the witness. That is on the 2000. So all the people who were present are named and listed on the cover sheet of those statements. And the May 8th - yesterday - again, the names of all persons present are on the sheet. The witness may not know the functions of these people, but he would know their names. He would have been introduced to them. I can assist, if the court wants, to tell what these people's functions were but that's not my purpose now. I just want to be fair to the witness that the name is Coo, Philip Coo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's time to adjourn now in any event. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue, I wish to ask you not to have the Prosecutor answer my questions, please, because I had a reason why I asked the witness who attended the interview; and what the first page says, I can read myself. Secondly, since we are already discussing that, I had expected you to react, in all fairness, because the witness is testifying according to your Rule 92 bis. Then the subject of the testimony and of the examination and cross-examination can only be that which is contained in his statement. And the Prosecutor introduced, during his introductory examination, some kind of a deportation map, although the witness in his statement did not testify about any deportations. As a matter of fact, the witness asserts in his statement that he saw the valley of Carragojs after the operations of the 28th. And the Prosecutor questioned him about the direction in which the refugees were moving, et cetera, et cetera. I would like to draw your attention to the following as well, since you said yourself that you are familiar with the statement - and I imagine this is your duty - and he says explicitly in the statement that he saw the valley of Carragojs after the operations of the 12th. This is what it says on page 12 in the penultimate paragraph of the statement, the statement given on the 12th of February, that is. And now I'm going to continue my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just deal with those matters. First of all, the interruption by the Prosecutor was by way of clarification, in particular because the name of the person present at the interview was not correctly pronounced. And the Prosecutor's entitled to do that. As for the deportation, there is evidence about that in the statement, and the witness was entitled to produce his map. Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I just wanted to assist the Court. Paragraph 59 of the second statement deals with the issue. There's some complaint about what I did; paragraph 59 of the second statement, page 19, completely -- oh, it's page 12 of 19. It says, "page of 19." It's page 12 of 19, paragraph 59. You'll see that that paragraph amply covers what was summarised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It refers to the annotated map of the operations in the valley in the Meja area and says he's provided it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, and it also talks about forcibly displacing civilians towards the paramilitary groups around Meja. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this does not bring into question what the statement says, that he saw this after the operation of the 28th, and I've just quoted to you where that was from. In the statement itself, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is the following: Are you afraid of the KLA now?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I have never been afraid of KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a long time during your military service, you were in a transport unit. You were a supervisor there, head of a squad within it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It is true that for four and a half years I was responsible for transportation, and for one year I was the chief responsible for transportation unit in Prishtina barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I could understand what you said, you were in charge of supplying vehicles, equipment, everything else that goes with the job; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was also responsible for training the drivers, planning, and such issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that from December 1998 onwards, you trained soldiers. You -- you planned the training and exercises, to put it more precisely. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of training was it? What subject?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Always related to transportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were actually preparing some plans, maps, for guards; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: When I was responsible in the operational training sector, after I was rotated from my first job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This planning, this planning the assignments of guards, the physical safety, security of the building, did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The physical safety of the facilities, that is, of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means I've understood you correctly. So you never had a position in the army that made it possible to you to have available to you any kind of information that relates to numbers of soldiers, deployment of troops, command, et cetera; isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That is not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You are saying that you were in charge of the security of the building. Do you mean that you were driving people from the command or providing physical security for persons? You worked on physical security. You were not involved in security matters within the army itself; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I was officer in charge of operational training sector where teaching, drilling plans are prepared, the division of the guards for the buildings are prepared and such issues, but not in the security in the sense of what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you a minute ago whether we can state that you were not in a position to have any kind of information made available to you that had to do with the number of troops, their deployment, reporting, et cetera. You said that was not correct. Tell me, in which sense did you have this kind of information made available to you, this information that pertains to the deployment of troops, command, reporting, et cetera, if you say that what I said on the basis of your statement was not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In the sector I used to work, I was not alone. There was the chief and another officer. But all the notes with the exception of some secret ones, all the notes, all the information was there, the number of soldiers, the kinds of weapons, vehicles, all the information was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You are talking about reservists of the army of Yugoslavia. Were there any Albanians among them?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes. At a later phase, very few. You might count them by the fingers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You claim that the members of the MUP and the reservists - actually, you even mentioned some paramilitaries - you claim that they committed some kind of crimes and that they got out of the command of the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The regular army was increased in numbers with those reservists who were on the lists of the army. Likewise, the police also has its reservists that it can draft now and again when it needs them. But there were also various volunteers, because some refused to join military formations. Therefore, they were obliged to draft anyone - terrorists, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. delinquents, former convicts, people with problems - and enlist them and bring them to Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to suggest that the authorities released criminals from prison so that they would join the army? Do you know of any such cases?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: We had problems all the time with such kinds of persons in Gjakove. The army imprisoned such persons. And on the basis of information we had, we found out that these were -- such persons were sent to prison for various offences, especially for criminal offences. And we had several such cases. They have created problems in the city, with the regular army soldiers especially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's clarify one matter. Reservists who came were included in the regular units. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Some were included in the regular units. I said that the regular units were fulfilled in numbers by -- with these reservists, but there were those who showed up on a voluntary basis through those other formations like the Tigers of Arkan or the Orlovi, the White Eagles of Seselj, and they also joined. They came on a voluntary basis to commit various offences, crimes, to plunder, to rob houses, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that, according to your assertion, there were reservists who came and who did not join the normal regular army units, that they were some kind of special units?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: First they came to the military units. Then, seeing that they could not abide by the discipline, they decided to leave and join these forces that I mentioned. So this is how the army came to have problems with them, let alone the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since you were an active officer and since you worked at the command, are you acquainted with the order on the ban of paramilitary formations which says that wherever they appear, they have to be arrested, disarmed, and disbanded? Are you aware of that order?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I am aware of the order. Then why didn't you arrest them in real terms when you knew what was happening on the basis of reports that came to you from the ground? So what did you do, you and all your command? We could do nothing, only to kill each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the commanders of the army of Yugoslavia arrested many soldiers, even those belonging to the regular force and to the reserve force, those who had committed some crimes?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It is true that we have arrested some, I know very well in Gjakove. But on the third day, at the most, orders came from above to release them. I know of one case when the guard told me - he was an old sergeant - it was a prison made up in a private home, in the cellar, he said at that orders came for us to release them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who could have issued these orders for you to release them when you said yourself a minute ago that you were aware of this order of the Supreme Command that such persons should be arrested?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: From what I heard from the person who told me - his name is Sergej Perovic - they had received this order from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that -- that soldiers who were suspected of having committed rapes were detained, tried, and ultimately convicted? Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That is correct. There was a case in Gllogofc village in Gjakove. It was the beginning of the arrests. And they were reservists of the regular army forces. That is a fact. But I don't know of any other cases of someone being convicted. I know of them being released later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you didn't say that anybody was later released, and you don't speak about one case but of several cases. And I'm drawing your attention to that page 4, paragraph 1, your statement of the 18th of April. So tell me, when were you telling the truth, then or now?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I said that these people who were imprisoned were convicted, but in other cases, they were released. This is what you haven't understood. I didn't say that people were imprisoned and convicted and not released, but the others, who were imprisoned later, were released. So this wasn't the first imprisonment. These imprisonments went on and measures were not taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that no measures were taken?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I saw in the evenings, when I visited the guards, I saw in the prison that I saw the same person with two other people, drinking in -- drinking beer in the Pashtrik Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that the commanders of the Yugoslav army did not order any violence, especially not rapes, and that things of that kind were highly isolated cases? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: As far as commanders of the regular army are concerned, it is true that they never -- I have never heard of them giving such an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's true. Now, is it also true what you claim, that every municipality had to have a police unit composed of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: At one time, at various centres, so-called local police were formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that members of that local police force in the villages were elected by the villagers themselves?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know who selected them because I didn't take part in these meetings or elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, they should have taken care of -- they were supposed to take care of the security in the villages and safety in the villages, to provide that. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I was never involved in any way in work of the police and of security, and no doubt they had their tasks allocated to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's something you talk about on page 5, the last paragraph in your statement from the 12th to the 15th of February, 2001. So that's what I'm asking you; is that correct or is it not, what you say there, it took care of the security of the villages, the Albanian policemen. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Reason would dictate such a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that you know of no orders for liquidation?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I never saw any such order for liquidation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your statement that there was a lot of drinking. Is it true that your commander ordered you to make this impossible, to see to it that it was not done?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. In the Pashtrik Hotel, Arkan's forces and the forces of Seselj and Frenki were stationed there, and the regular army was not normally allowed to go there. But they never asked anybody, but they created havoc and fired guns. And by order -- the order was to go and take a few guards and to close it and stop the serving of alcohol, but it was impossible to get them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not act upon those orders, did you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I went back and told the commander what the situation was like, and then the chief of the brigade became angry and said I should go -- that he would go. And he fared worse, because he was seen off by whistles and firing in the air. And he left and came back to his base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned Seselj, Arkan. You mentioned these names and the names of several individuals. Now, do you know that neither Seselj nor Arkan were ever in Kosovo during the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: During the war, I never saw them in Kosova. They were there before the war, but their men under their command, as is well known, were there. And they said themselves that they were also in Bosnia and Croatia. And they would come to the hotel every day and contact soldiers who were there, and they would admit, themselves, who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if somebody says something about themselves, does that mean that it must necessarily be correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There was an entire unit there. It wasn't a matter of a single individual. There were dozens there. They were housed in the Pashtrik Hotel. These were Arkan's men and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. I'm asking you this because you're saying some things which are absolutely impossible. For example, you talk about Frenki's men, the Frenkis. Now, who are these people who called themselves Frenki's men or the Frenkis? And what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Frenki was a unit, the most terrorist unit possible that committed acts of the terror, together with Arkan's men. And I also heard from my other former colleagues that they were people without parents, people who had grown up in orphanages, people without feeling. They would kill someone as if slaughtering a chicken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that what you're claiming would not have been possible at all because Frenki or, rather, Franko was no kind of paramilitary formation, it was a deputy to the chief of security who, earlier on, was the head of a regular Anti-Terrorist Unit? So that it was absolutely impossible that what you call bandits should be the members of a unit of this kind. Do you know that, as an officer?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I can say quite seriously that this was a special unit with a commander from Belgrade who -- who himself told -- the commander himself told me not to get mixed up with them, not to have any business -- not to do any business with them and not to have anything to do with them. And their commander went among houses in the city and was involved in torture of various kinds. And I don't know what kind of unit it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Is it clear that that man was no Frenki, or, rather, somebody that people called Frenki?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know Frenki personally, and I don't know who he is, but the unit as a whole was known as Frenki, and they had black scarves around their heads, and they wore different uniforms; the police, army special forces, semi-civilian, semi-military, all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means, in fact, that that could not have been a unit Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. belonging to the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, the security service. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I can say, according to the conversations that I had with any former colleagues with whom I talked at length about these matters, that they were commanded directly by someone from the secret ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know, as an officer of the Yugoslav army, that the Anti-Terrorist Unit and the security service is the most highly disciplined unit that is made up of people who were sportsmen, if I can say that, with high physical and mental capabilities? So highly disciplined and well-organised unit. And it cannot correspond to a picture as you depicted it.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's -- indeed it's true as you say. They were physically very well-built and muscular and well fit to commit crimes of various kinds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you claim that that unit was precisely that, what you tried to explain by saying that it was a part of the service of the interior?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I'm sure that they committed crimes, and I don't believe I have need to go into any details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's very important to know whether you're talking about some, shall I say, group of criminals or whether you're talking about a unit which belongs to the organs of power and authority of the Republic of Serbia. That is a very vital point for what you're testifying about. I assume you are well aware of the fact, as an officer, that this kind of testimony paints a very ugly picture of the regular forces of the powers that be, if what you're saying were to be true.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe or what name to put to it, but that was a unit that committed crimes. For me, this can be called only a criminal group. I know of no other names to call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What did you see the unit doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This unit, in cooperation with some in Gjakove city, they were stationed near the stadium called Vllaznimi stadium. All night, they used to set fire to houses in various areas of the city. During the day, at about 14 hours, they gathered in the coffeeshop called Rinia, which was situated across from the army house. When it became dark, they continued the same operations. We could -- we only saw the flames coming out of various houses in the city. They -- we heard rifle shots. I could see that. I could hear that because my guards were nearby where these -- near the army building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, didn't you say a moment ago that in fact it wasn't a unit, it was group of criminals? Wasn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I said they belonged to this unit called Frenki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it clear to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Peraj, did you personally know the name of Franko Simatovic or as to what he was doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew only the name, only the name. I know nothing of what he may have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you're saying here yourself loud and clear, isn't it clear to you that it is impossible for a group of that kind to be any kind of regular unit, especially not an elite unit of the security forces? Isn't that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't say that it is a unit of the regular army or something of the sort. I only said that they acted together as a unit, called Frenki. That was how it was known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, somebody gave them that name or they gave themselves that name, but it couldn't have had anything to do with the security service as such. Is that clear to you, as an officer of the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I -- I am afraid I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did the unit have any connection, that you could see, with the regular forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you just said that it couldn't have had any connection with the regular forces in response to the question asked by Mr. May, and as you said previously that it was obviously a group of criminals, and as you were in charge of security, why, then, didn't you arrest them?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Efforts were made to arrest not only them but others who committed crimes in the city. But it was impossible. I said earlier that the commander of the barracks went there, but he failed because they were so many in numbers that we didn't know what problems we might expect from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that for the MUP, it was the colonel of the Yugoslav army who was responsible and that his name was Djosen, if I read the name correctly here. Djosen. Now, what does a colonel of the Yugoslav army have to do with the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior? How do you explain that observation of yours?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Colonel Milan Djosen, he was a commander of the garrison and of the brigade of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he wasn't in charge of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: At war times, the commander of a garrison becomes the number one person in that garrison. This applies to the police and to other forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Djosen order you to address the criminals?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Not to arrest them but to stop the hotel serving them beer and to send them away from that hotel, to make them go to some other place where they were supposed to be stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There's no sense in pursuing that topic, but I hope that everything is clear. You mentioned Generals Pavkovic, Lazarevic in your statement. However, as it is not clear of the context you mention them in, can we take it that you never actually met Pavkovic and Lazarevic personally?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I met Pavkovic at least 200 times, but Lazarevic less often because he came later to Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let's clarify the character of those meetings. You were in charge of security, providing security for the command building. Now, the fact that you met -- did you meet him when he was coming in and out of the building and you would see him, or were you reporting to him as head of security to tell him that the situation was normal, reporting in that way, or did you just see him going in and out of the building? So is that how you met him? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I met him, as I said, because during my stay in Prishtina, I was looking after the garrison, and I reported every morning about the situation in the garrison, and he would summon me to give me jobs to do during the day, so I had regular contact with him. And also with Lazarevic. He was his deputy in Prishtina when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they regular and proper official contacts which an officer in charge of security would have with his -- with the commander in chief for that area?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that some volunteers from Russia arrived. And subsequently this morning, I saw in some of the corrections that you were making that was read out by Mr. Ryneveld, that you corrected that statement and said that there were nine people, that there was a doctor amongst them from Russia. So this group, according to the corrections you made to your statement, it would appear was a sort of humanitarian group. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It was a group that was armed and in camouflage uniform. They were volunteers, and they had reported as volunteers. And we received them in the basement of the palace of culture in Gjakove and registered them and allocated them units to go to. And this unit was taken to Koshare, on the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that the commander of your unit refused to receive them, to receive the request for them to remain in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The commander told them, through the administrative officer that was there, and I was very close to the commander when he said, "No. You must go into combat if you are volunteers, because we have plenty of people to loot in the city."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that he deployed them as volunteers along the border in Kosare to supervise the border?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There was fighting taking place there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about Kosare there, and I assume you're talking about the border point of Kosare -- the border post of Kosare.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that during the NATO aggression, meetings were held of the army and MUP and the Territorial Defence. Did you at any time, and if so in what capacity, attend meetings of that kind?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I was at these meetings several times. And they told me to go and check the guards. And sometimes I would come in by accident and see the meetings going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, your statement doesn't show that you attended any official meeting with -- that was attended by such people.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They were more like briefings and consultations, because the time and circumstances didn't permit any proper meetings. They were merely meetings for information and allocating duties and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it logical that at a time of war, the responsible officers of the army and police exchange information mutually, precisely the way you put it just now?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's normal. It's in the normal course of business. If everything else had been normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that in the area of Kosovo, there were 150.000 soldiers deployed. You never saw this figure officially, you never heard it officially, and you did not hold the kind of position that would make it possible for you to know that for sure. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: My colleagues said this, my senior colleagues, that there are about 150.000 troops in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that as for operations against the KLA, there were persons responsible in the army of Yugoslavia. Are you claiming, when you say this, that the MUP did not have any clashes with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: MUP was involved in more conflicts than the army. These are conflicts with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, clashes with the KLA. I just wanted to check what this explanation of yours meant, that it was the army that was responsible for the KLA. You did not mention the MUP. Of course this was against the KLA. Now let's move on to the next question. You try, in your statement, to explain or, rather, provide some information about the army of Yugoslavia. For example, about the mode of information, about, for example, information from Nis going to the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade. If you're already dealing with these facts and figures, could you please describe who sent information to who. Or to begin with, who was Minister of Defence at that time who received information from Nis, who had information from Nis sent to him?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Information came from the -- went from the lowest rank to the highest rank, according to the command structure. Of course, every barracks in Kosova sent reports to the commander of the Pristina Corps. The commander of the corps to the army in Nis and from thence to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now you're stating -- all right. You're actually explaining now that information flows were regularly within the regular chain of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that technical equipment arrived in Djakovica from Republika Srpska. Is it correct that you do not know this for sure? Is it correct that this is only your assumption?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There are grounds for thinking this because, according to an agreement which you know better than I do, the weaponry was downsized, and the units were specified, especially the tank units and the heavy military equipment. So if -- if one unit gave heavy equipment to another, I heard that these units had equipment that they brought themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that, at that time - at this time that you are testifying about - just like today, after all, the entire territory of Republika Srpska is under SFOR control in the military sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it was like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you assume that under such circumstances, there is a possibility for tanks, personnel carriers, combat vehicles to be transferred from Republika Srpska to the territory of Kosovo without SFOR knowing anything about it, without SFOR seeing it, making it impossible, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
